prompt:
Extract a SysML v2 model from the document as a list of facts. Each fact has unit_id (the sentence it comes from), type and slots. Give only the slots that have a value, as a list of {slot, value} pairs; for composition give one 'parts' pair per part.

Types and slots:
  attribute(owner,name,value,unit) action(performer,label) state(owner,label) constraint(subject,expression) requirement(subject,text)
  composition(whole,parts) flow(source,target,payload) succession(before,after) transition(from,to,trigger) allocation(action,to)

Name each element by its full name as first introduced in the document.
RULES:
- Resolve every entity-valued slot using all the text you are given. If a sentence refers to an element by an alias, abbreviation, pronoun or shorter description, write the element's full name as first introduced. If a sentence says an element receives or uses an item and the text you are given states which element produces or sends that item, emit a flow from that producer to the receiver. If an element cannot be determined from the text you are given, use null; never guess.
- Never write placeholder words such as "any", "all", "some state" for an unstated element; use null.
- Do not merge differently named things unless the text says they are the same.
- Emit one action for EVERY behavior verb phrase, including passive voice (performer null), capability statements, displays, logs, generates and reports. label = the verbatim verb phrase with its object.
- Emit a requirement for every NORMATIVE statement (shall, must, should, will, is required to, needs to). Purpose, goal or benefit sentences are not requirements.
- Emit a state for every named mode or state; transitions use the state names, with from null when the prior state is not stated.
- Emit a succession only for an EXPLICIT temporal connective between two actions ("then", "after", "once", "before", "when ... is complete", "next", "finally"); before/after are the action labels. Never use succession for cause or data transfer.
- Resolve a pronoun or "this/these" performer to the element named in the preceding sentence and write that element's name; if it cannot be resolved, use null. Never output a pronoun as a slot value.
- Drop determiners and quantifiers from element names ("Each Soil Moisture Probe" -> "Soil Moisture Probe", "the system" -> "system").
- allocation.to must be a component or actor, never a mode or state.
- Emit a constraint for every threshold, limit, period or deadline stated with a number; expression = the verbatim phrase.
- Emit a flow for every sentence in which an element sends, transmits, reports, displays, commands or delivers an item (target null if the receiver is not named).
 Also list under "entities" every system element, actor or item named in the document units, with its full name and any alias the text explicitly declares for it (e.g. 'hereafter X', 'known as X', 'called X'); aliases [] if none. Return JSON {"entities": [...], "facts": [...]}.

Memory from EARLIER parts of the document (do not extract facts from it; use it only to resolve names, aliases and who produces an item):
Document: Management by Trajectory (MBT) concept for future air traffic management (ATM) in the National Airspace System (NAS). Current NAS: ATM system holds a predicted trajectory per flight from the approved flight plan plus scheduled/controlled departure time. Controllers tactically manage airborne aircraft via 'open trajectory' vectors, altitude and speed clearances to implement restrictions, separate aircraft and address NAS constraints. Strategic flight plan changes are conservative, so weather reroutes and new Traffic Flow Management (TFM) restrictions are left to controllers. Tactical actions are not communicated to automation or other stakeholders, degrading prediction of constraint impacts and demand at NAS resources. Ground Delay Programs (GDPs) and Airspace Flow Programs (AFPs) assign departure times to meet a Controlled Time of Arrival (CTA) at a constraint using the airspace user's estimated time en route, without knowledge of controller actions. Time Based Flow Management (TBFM) assumes estimated times of arrival (ETAs) are correct. MBT: the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) and airspace users negotiate four-dimensional trajectories (4DTs) for all flights, respecting user goals and NAS constraints; negotiated 4DTs communicate the traffic management plan. Accommodates traditional commercial aviation and emerging users: Unmanned Aircraft Systems, space vehicles, on-demand air transportation vehicles. Pilots and controllers use automation to keep aircraft on the assigned trajectory, including temporal/speed constraints; equipped aircraft are substantially responsible for compliance without controller intervention. Assigned trajectories respect all known constraints from current location to destination. NAS constraint impacts are inserted into the assigned trajectory as trajectory constraints, eliminating most local reactive control actions; uncertainty/disruptions are resolved by proactive trajectory (constraint) modifications as far in advance as possible. Enablers: improved ground and aircraft automation, air-ground and ground-ground data communications. MBT resembles Trajectory Based Operations (TBO) concepts using a 4D contract; appendix compares with International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) TBO. TBO meanings: high-level vision with 4DTs at the core of ATC/ATM; and evolving set of endeavors toward it. Actors: FAA, airspace users, pilots, controllers, ATM automation, aircraft automation, other stakeholders.

Document units:
U0027: MBT is one specific interpretation of the high-level TBO vision, and is the starting point from which specific challenges can be identified and studied, contributing to the refinement of the MBT concept and the overall body of knowledge related to TBO. 1.1 NAS Shortfalls Addressed by MBT This section summarizes the shortfalls in the current NAS that are addressed by MBT, as shown in Table 1.
U0028: These shortfalls are consistent with those identified in the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) TBO Concept Document [1].
U0029: The ICAO TBO Concept Document provides high-level guidance for resolving these shortfalls, and the MBT concept provides a specific vision for resolving the shortfalls that is consistent with the ICAO TBO Concept.
U0030: Table 1.
U0031: NAS Shortfalls Addressed by MBT Shortfalls MBT Improvements Data exchanged between airspace users and the FAA are too sparse to support accurate trajectory prediction across all phases of flight and trajectory synchronization across automation systems.
U0032: The data needed by all relevant airspace users, aircraft, and FAA automation systems to develop accurate, consistent 4DT predictions are available to all relevant systems.
U0033: The use of open trajectories, including tactical maneuvers, causes poor trajectory predictability.
U0034: Aircraft operate on closed trajectories to the extent possible, which improves trajectory predictability.
U0035: Insufficient publication of trajectory changes and lack of trajectory synchronization result in poor trajectory predictability.
U0036: Publication of all trajectory changes and advanced exchange of trajectory information between ground automation systems and the aircraft allow for trajectory synchronization across systems, resulting in consistent trajectory predictions across systems.
U0037: Poor trajectory predictability inhibits strategic (longer look ahead) trajectory management.
U0038: Improved trajectory predictability, improved coordination capabilities, and use of 4DTs enable controllers to use strategic, closed clearances.
U0039: A high level of trajectory predictability becomes the new norm.
U0040: Enhanced predictability will improve TFM performance and provide a more consistent flow of air traffic, where demand will more accurately meet available capacity, reducing or eliminating delay.
U0041: All applicable NAS constraints, both dynamic (e.g., TFM) and static (e.g., crossing restrictions) are published such that they can be known by all airspace users and relevant automation systems.
